newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea life insurance industry seen restructuring.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea life insurance industry seen restructuring.

text.p: South Korea's deeply troubled life insurance industry could suffer a shake-out if the country's top five conglomerates or chaebols are allowed to participate in the sector, analysts said on Thursday.
The Presidential Commission for Financial Reform has recommended that the top five chaebols be allowed to establish life insurance companies.
That proposal, announced on Tuesday, would open the door for the Hyundai, LG, Daewoo and Sunkyong groups to compete with the powerful Samsung Life Insurance Co.
Currently, Samsung Group is the only major chaebol with a life insurance company under its wing. Samsung set up its insurer years before big groups were banned from the business.

"Backed with abundant funds and powerful networks, chaebols' participation will generate hot competition. I expect the life insurance business to restructure," said Mok Young-choong, analyst at ING Barings.
Some life insurers are already shaky, he said.
Proposals to President Kim Young-sam for sweeping reforms in the nation's backward financial industry focused more on modernising the local banking industry than insurance.
But the finance ministry is expected to submit to parliament in June legislation that would deregulate South Korea's life insurance market.

As part of that deregulation, the minimum capital requirement for life insurers would be raised to 30 billion won ($33.67 million) from 10 billion. But the requirement for non-life insurers would remain unchanged at 30 billion won.

Chaebols would be allowed to establish a new life insurance company only if they acquired at least one insolvent life insurer. Otherwise, they could get into the business by merging more than two insolvent insurers.
"The government is trying to use the top five chaebols to help improve the insolvency problem in the life-insurance business," said Lee Hwa-yeol, Ssangyong Securities analyst.
Most of the 33 life insurers operating in South Korea -- the world's sixth biggest life insurance market -- are thought by analysts to be technically insolvent.
"Lapse levels in the life market are a major factor affecting the industry's solvency," said Geoff Barrs, managing director of actuarial consultants NMG Pte Ltd in Singapore.
"Very little of the business sticks for any decent period so it's almost impossible for companies to make any money."
An official at the Korea Life Insurance Association said regulators set the solvency margin requirement for life insurers at one percent over policy reserves.
But 27 of 33 life insurers had a policy reserve shortage totalling 1.2 trillion won at the end of March, 1995, according to the most recent figures available, he said.
Concerns over the solvency of South Korean life insurers have been raised in the wake of the 200 billion yen ($1.58 billion) failure in April of Japan's Nissan Mutual Life.
With deregulation, the number of life insurers shot up to 33 at present, including joint ventures and regional insurers, compared with seven in 1988.
But analysts said few are profitable.
"Newcomers seemed to think they would be able to make a big fortune in life insurance," Lee said.
"But they did not realise they would have to pay excessive operating expenses for buildings, solicitors and so forth in order to survive Korea's fierce competition."
The association official said Hyundai and LG appeared most interested in entering the life insurance industry.

"Owning banks has been almost impossible so far and securities houses are not profitable. But with life insurance, chaebols think they will be able to improve cash-flow in the group," the official said.
(Conversion $1 = 891.00)
